Brainy Dr Amy Martin

By: Laura Byrne | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Carte Blanche meets an extraordinary young woman who is living with only 75% of her brain...and has just graduated with a PhD

Unique Selling Point:
Amy Martin battled through her teenage years with recurrent, rare brain tumours. She underwent three operations to remove the tumours and address the severe epilepsy that was a side effect, resulting in the loss of 25% of her brain. Despite this and the many challenges and effects of the cancer, she has thrived, and in April this year, graduated with her PhD in Ancient Cultures from Stellenbosch University.

Summary:
When Amy was just 14 she began to experience difficulty speaking and paralysis down the left side of her body. After a trip to a neurologist, she was diagnosed with juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma, and her long battle for health began. An operations to remove the tumour left her facing the possibility she may never regain full mobility.

And the fight was only just beginning. The tumour caused severe epilepsy, and recurred when Amy was 17. Further operations were needed, leaving her with four titanium plates and 16 titanium screws in her skull. She struggled at school with bullying when her dramatic surgery scars were visible, and dared not leave the house for fear she would have a seizure. She was also missing a full 25% of her brain.

But Amy didn't give up. Finally in the clear by her early 20s, she turned her gaze on the future and enrolled at Stellenbosch University to study languages and culture. She found her feet at university and became part of campus life. After her undergraduate, she went to South Korea to teach English for two years, then returned to complete her Honours and Masters. After another stint in South Korea, she embarked on her PhD in ancient cultures, and finally graduated in April 2022. Her thesis focused on the notion of a female poetic tradition in ancient Greek literature.

Besides her academic career, Amy also loves jogging and watching movies. She's learning Korean and is about to leave South Africa to return to South Korea a third time.

Further information:
1. Juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma (JPA)
Juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma is a rare form of childhood tumour (technically not a cancer), affecting an estimated 14 per million children under 15. However, it is the most common form of brain tumour in children. Most cases occur in the first two decades of life, and most (80%) are low grade tumours, which means they are benign, slow-growing, and do not spread to the surrounding brain tissue. The usual form of treatment is surgery to remove the tumour. Follow-up radiation may be required if not all of the tumour can be removed.

Most JPAs develop in the cerebellum (which controls movement), the brainstem, the hypothalamic region or the optic nerve pathways, although they can occur anywhere in the central nervous system. The most common result is increased intracranial pressure, and symptoms can include headaches, lethargy, vomiting, personality changes, seizures, vision problems, and muscle weakness.

2. Living with a partial brain
Surprisingly, there are many documented cases of people living normal lives despite the fact that they are missing substantial chunks of their brains. In one case, in 2014, a woman walked into a hospital in China complaining of dizziness and nausea - only for scans to show that she was missing her entire cerebellum. This area is believed to be responsible for muscle control, but the woman could walk, despite some clumsiness.

In another case, a French man in his 40s went to hospital complaining of some weakness in one leg. Scans revealed that the entire inner part of his brain was missing - apparently eroded over years by a fluid build-up. The man had a low IQ but was not mentally disabled, had a job as a civil servant, and was married with children.

It seems that we do not know enough about the brain and the functions of its various areas. It seems that unlike human technology, there is a lot of crossover in function between different regions, and perhaps working regions are able to step in when a vital part is missing.

Press Release:


Mind Over Matter
At 14 years old, Amy Martin began to experience weakness and difficulty moving the left side of her body. A neurologist confirmed a devastating diagnosis: Juvenile Pilocytic Astrocytoma – a rare brain tumour affecting children. An operation to remove the tumour left her suffering from severe epilepsy and unsure whether she’d ever regain full mobility. By her early twenties, and after two more brain surgeries, Amy had four titanium plates and 16 titanium screws in her skull and was missing about a quarter of her brain. But she didn't give up, turning her gaze towards the future and enrolling at Stellenbosch University. In April this year, Amy graduated with a PhD in ancient cultures - a thrilling climax for the woman with just 75 percent of her brain.
Producer: Laura Byrne | Presenter: Claire Mawisa

Script:


EXCERPT: GRADUATION VIDEO: Amy Martin with dissertation Poetess on the Periphery: revisiting the female poetic tradition in Hellenistic poetry.
UPSOUND: BARRY MARTIN: For me, seeing her walk onto that stage… Emotional. The best moment of my life.
VOICEOVER: This April, 33 year-old Western Cape local Amy Martin graduated with her PhD from Stellenbosch University. Her thesis re-examined the role of female poets in Ancient Greece.
UPSOUND: AMY MARTIN: My dad always took us on field trips to go and see fossils in the Cederberg. So I can attribute my passion and my love for the ancient world to my father…
UPSOUND: BARRY MARTIN: She did her PhD at this very table that we’re sitting at now. I brought her coffee, I made her food. And look where we are.
LINK: Globally, only one percent of university graduates have a PhD – it’s an achievement beyond most of us. But Dr Amy Martin has overcome a lot more than you or me to get to this point.
VOICEOVER: In fact, a quarter of Amy’s skull is filled not with brain tissue but spinal fluid. She was only 14 when her normal, healthy childhood was brutally interrupted.
UPSOUND: AMY MARTIN: I was having dinner with my family one evening and the fork fell out of my hand.
UPSOUND: BARRY MARTIN: She complained of headaches, blurred vision, dizziness, balance problems.
VOICEOVER: Her father, Barry, remembers receiving the news: an MRI scan had revealed a large tumour inside Amy’s skull.
UPSOUND: BARRY MARTIN: Obviously, it just took the wind out my sails. And, you know, you have visions of your daughter losing her life.
UPSOUND: AMY MARTIN: Everything happened so fast. The one moment they did an MRI and the next morning I was in the hospital and a few days later I had my first brain operation.
VOICEOVER: The tumour was a rare but benign juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma. Luckily, it was in an accessible part of her brain, so it was successfully removed. But little did Amy know this was only the beginning of the journey.
UPSOUND: AMY MARTIN: About a year after I had my first brain operation, I was diagnosed with epilepsy. And that was probably the biggest challenge that I had to face.
VOICEOVER: The severity of her seizures left Amy afraid to leave the house.
UPSOUND: BARRY MARTIN: We were always conscious of it, almost 24 seven. My other daughter, Nina, she's very sporty, so we would go to the school and sometimes she had an epileptic fit right there next to the netball court. And it was difficult to deal with, especially for her.
VOICEOVER: The quest for a solution brought Amy to neurosurgeon Dr Roger Melvill, who discovered that the tumour had grown back.
UPSOUND: DR ROGER MELVILL: We open the skull and we slide these electrodes over the surface of the brain, and then that wire comes out to be monitored. And from that information, it's possible to return to remove the tumour and also remove brain tissue which is close to the tumour, that is the cause of the epilepsy.
VOICEOVER: But this meant a third procedure that came with major risks.
UPSOUND: DR ROGER MELVILL: This over here is the part of the brain responsible for moving arm and leg. So if the surgeon travels into that part of the brain, then the person ends up having paralysis. And if the surgeon goes too far back into this occipital area, there may be significant disturbance in vision.
UPSOUND: AMY MARTIN: He absolutely saved my life. You know, it wasn't just a case of taking the tumour away so that I could live, but actually offering me a normal, healthy, stable life. Because you can survive with epilepsy, right? With seizures. But it's a very low quality of life.
LINK: This is a scan of Amy’s brain. The tumour affected the parietal area, and once it was removed, it left the massive cavity we see here.
UPSOUND: DR ROGER MELVILL: If we were to operate on you in this area, not being quite as young as Amy.
CLAIRE MAWISA: But not much older, but not much older!
DR ROGER MELVILL: Then you might have difficulty with orientating yourself. You know, you get up to go to the kitchen and you find yourself in the bathroom by mistake.
VOICEOVER: However, in a young person like Amy, the brain is able to compensate for the loss of tissue through a process called plasticity.
UPSOUND: AMY MARTIN: Family members make jokes - she has a screw loose in her head because of course, I have titanium screws and plates in my head.
CLAIRE MAWISA: Do you really?
AMY MARTIN: Yes. And I do still struggle with my balance. I do experience dizziness now and then, and severe headaches now and then. But ultimately, I live a healthy, normal life.
VOICEOVER: After more than a decade, scans show no recurrence of the tumour and Amy has thrown herself into her future. She’s working on a book based on her PhD research, and in just a few days she heads back to South Korea for a third stint as an English instructor.
UPSOUND: AMY MARTIN: I promised myself that if I survive all of this, that I was going to see the world.
UPSOUND: BARRY MARTIN: She lives life harder than most people who've never had any of these problems.
UPSOUND: AMY MARTIN: I was terrified for a few years after my brain operations. I lived a very secluded, very cautious life. But today I challenge myself to open myself up to, you know, new challenges. And that's just the best I can do.

PROMOS

PROMO 1 (21 SECS)
UPSOUND: AMY MARTIN: I didn't allow this tumour to define me in any way.
VOICEOVER: Imagine losing a large part of your brain to surgery for recurrent tumours…but the rest works so well that, a decade later, you graduate with a PhD.
UPSOUND: BARRY MARTIN: Amy was always going to achieve something. And I'm just proud that I could have taken part of that journey with her.

PROMO 2 (21 SECS)
VOICEOVER: Getting a PhD is a rare achievement at the best of times. Add a long battle with tumours that left a large defect in her brain, and Dr Amy Martin’s accomplishments invite applause.
UPSOUND: AMY MARTIN: But you don't allow it to overwhelm you. You just see it as an opportunity to live life to the full.

PROMO 3 (11 SECS)
LINK: How is it possible for anyone to function normally with a substantial chunk of their brain missing?
VOICEOVER: I meet the extraordinary Dr Amy Martin to find out.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Carte Blanche meets an extraordinary young woman who is living with only 75% of her brain...and has just graduated with a PhD
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Amy Martin battled through her teenage years with recurrent, rare brain tumours. She underwent three operations to remove the tumours and address the severe epilepsy that was a side effect, resulting in the loss of 25% of her brain. Despite this and the many challenges and effects of the cancer, she has thrived, and in April this year, graduated with her PhD in Ancient Cultures from Stellenbosch University.
metadata.Summary: When Amy was just 14 she began to experience difficulty speaking and paralysis down the left side of her body. After a trip to a neurologist, she was diagnosed with juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma, and her long battle for health began. An operations to remove the tumour left her facing the possibility she may never regain full mobility. And the fight was only just beginning. The tumour caused severe epilepsy, and recurred when Amy was 17. Further operations were needed, leaving her with four titanium plates and 16 titanium screws in her skull. She struggled at school with bullying when her dramatic surgery scars were visible, and dared not leave the house for fear she would have a seizure. She was also missing a full 25% of her brain. But Amy didn't give up. Finally in the clear by her early 20s, she turned her gaze on the future and enrolled at Stellenbosch University to study languages and culture. She found her feet at university and became part of campus life. After her undergraduate, she went to South Korea to teach English for two years, then returned to complete her Honours and Masters. After another stint in South Korea, she embarked on her PhD in ancient cultures, and finally graduated in April 2022. Her thesis focused on the notion of a female poetic tradition in ancient Greek literature. Besides her academic career, Amy also loves jogging and watching movies. She's learning Korean and is about to leave South Africa to return to South Korea a third time.
metadata.Further information: 1. Juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma (JPA) Juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma is a rare form of childhood tumour (technically not a cancer), affecting an estimated 14 per million children under 15. However, it is the most common form of brain tumour in children. Most cases occur in the first two decades of life, and most (80%) are low grade tumours, which means they are benign, slow-growing, and do not spread to the surrounding brain tissue. The usual form of treatment is surgery to remove the tumour. Follow-up radiation may be required if not all of the tumour can be removed. Most JPAs develop in the cerebellum (which controls movement), the brainstem, the hypothalamic region or the optic nerve pathways, although they can occur anywhere in the central nervous system. The most common result is increased intracranial pressure, and symptoms can include headaches, lethargy, vomiting, personality changes, seizures, vision problems, and muscle weakness. 2. Living with a partial brain Surprisingly, there are many documented cases of people living normal lives despite the fact that they are missing substantial chunks of their brains. In one case, in 2014, a woman walked into a hospital in China complaining of dizziness and nausea - only for scans to show that she was missing her entire cerebellum. This area is believed to be responsible for muscle control, but the woman could walk, despite some clumsiness. In another case, a French man in his 40s went to hospital complaining of some weakness in one leg. Scans revealed that the entire inner part of his brain was missing - apparently eroded over years by a fluid build-up. The man had a low IQ but was not mentally disabled, had a job as a civil servant, and was married with children. It seems that we do not know enough about the brain and the functions of its various areas. It seems that unlike human technology, there is a lot of crossover in function between different regions, and perhaps working regions are able to step in when a vital part is missing.
